title: Investigating High School and Pre-High School Teachers’ Perceptions and Experiences Introducing Quantum Concepts: A Survey of QuanTime and other Quantum-related Activities
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers perceive and experience the use of QuanTime and other quantum-related activities for introducing foundational quantum concepts. The central question is whether these packaged, ready-to-use activities are feasible, engaging, and curriculum-compatible for pre-high school and high school classrooms, and whether teachers see them as useful for building early quantum literacy and student interest in quantum science and technology.

The intervention/approach studied is a set of QuanTime quantum-learning activities and related quantum resources, which include hands-on, interactive lessons on topics such as wave-particle duality, electron transitions, art and polarization, entanglement, and quantum games. The study used a survey with 12 Likert-scale items and open-ended questions. Teachers were grouped into pre-high school (grades 4-8) and high school (grades 9-12) categories, and were recruited through the National Q-12 Education Partnership. Of 132 teachers contacted, 36 completed more than 60% of the survey; 12 were pre-high school teachers and 23 were high school teachers, with one additional outreach coordinator/informal educator.

Findings suggest generally positive teacher perceptions across both grade bands. Most teachers reported that the activities fit their curriculum, were manageable to implement, and engaged students without requiring substantial extra preparation or support. High school teachers tended to report slightly stronger agreement than pre-high school teachers on many items, including curriculum fit, student enjoyment, and classroom engagement. Teachers also expressed strong interest in using the activities again. Open-ended responses emphasized that the activities were easy to integrate, visually engaging, and useful for sparking curiosity, though some teachers noted that more support would help with more advanced questions and that younger students sometimes needed more time and scaffolding. Overall, the study concludes that QuanTime is a promising teacher-friendly resource for early quantum education in K-12 settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive survey study with self-selected respondents and no experimental comparison, so causal inference is limited. The paper provides useful implementation evidence, but it relies on teacher self-report rather than direct student outcome measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modestly positive implementation and engagement effects, but the impact is unclear because outcomes are based on perceptions rather than measured learning gains. The study is relevant to K-12 quantum education, yet it does not demonstrate medium or large effects on student achievement or broader system outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing packaged quantum science classroom activities (e.g., Wave-Particle Duality, Electron Transitions, Art & Polarization) used to introduce foundational quantum concepts in middle and high school lessons

finding.finding_summary: This survey study found that teachers viewed QuanTime and related quantum activities as supporting students' learning of foundational quantum concepts and their ability to discuss quantum phenomena. Across 36 respondents (12 pre-high school, 23 high school, plus 1 outreach coordinator), most teachers agreed that the activities fit their curriculum, were manageable to implement, and helped students engage with concepts such as wave-particle duality and electron transitions; average Likert ratings for perceived student learning/engagement were generally above 5.0 on a 7-point scale.
finding.measure: Teacher Likert-scale ratings and open-ended feedback on student learning, engagement, and interest in quantum concepts

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that students enjoyed and were engaged by the quantum activities, with particularly strong endorsement from high school teachers. On average, teachers rated student enjoyment at 5.8/7 and engagement at 5.7/7 overall, and 87% of high school teachers and 82% of pre-high school teachers said they would like to do the activities again next year.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student enjoyment, engagement, and willingness to repeat activities

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses suggested that the activities prompted curiosity, discussion, and collaborative work, especially around visually rich concepts like wave-particle duality and entanglement. Teachers noted students asking deeper questions and working in groups to collect results and plot graphs, indicating some support for critical thinking and collaboration, though these outcomes were not directly measured with standardized instruments.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher feedback on student questioning, group work, and sense-making

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported that the activities were easy to integrate and did not require substantial extra preparation or support. Mean ratings were 4.0/7 for needing more preparation time and 3.6/7 for wanting more support, suggesting low implementation burden; open-ended comments repeatedly described the materials as ready-to-use and simple to implement.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings on preparation time and implementation support; qualitative implementation feedback
